title: Stone Age
intro: Indian History General Studies B–9 Stone Age *The period without documented evidence of its history is called the Prehistoric period . Proto-historic period is the period having shreds of evidence of a script which is still not deciphered. Proto-historic refers to the period between prehistoric and historical periods. *The time after which we get a documented description is called historic period . *The Stone Age comes under the Prehistoric period. *Indus valley civilization and Copper Age culture come under the Proto-historic period. *The historical period starts from around 6th century B.C. *In India, the research on Stone Age Civilization started at ﬁ rst in 1863. The whole Stone Age has been categorized into three parts on the basis of diﬀ erence of tools used. These are Palaeolithic period, Mesolithic period and Neolithic period. *Palaeolithic Period is further categorized into three periods on the same basis- (i) The Lower Palaeolithic period -Handaxe, Cleaver, Chopper, etc. (ii) The Middle Palaeolithic period- Points, Borer, Scrapper (iii) The Upper Palaeolithic period - Burins, Blades *Chopper-Chopping pebble pieces of tools were at first obtained from Sohan river valley of Punjab (Pakistan). At ﬁ rst, hand-axe pieces of equipment were found in Pallavaram and Attirampakkam near Chennai (Tamil Nadu). Other tools of this culture are cleaver, scraper, etc. *Robert Bruce Foote was a British geologist and archaeologist. *The expedition of Yale Cambridge team under the leadership of De. Terra did the most important research in Sohan valley in 1935. *In Belan valley, the research was carried under the direction of G.R. Sharma of Allahabad University. Nearly 44 archaeological sites were found in this valley which is related to the Lower Palaeolithic period. *Apart from tools, the statue of bone-made Mother Goddess of this age was obtained from Lohanda Nala region of Belan Valley which is currently preserved at the Prayagraj museum. *The life of Palaeolithic people was natural. They were primarily dependent on hunting. They were unfamiliar with ﬁ re, so they ate raw meat. Palaeolithic people were unfamiliar with farming and animal husbandry . *We came to know about Mesolithic period after A.C.L. Carlleyle discovered (1867-68 A.D.) the Rock Painting from Vindhya region. *According to I. Ancient History of India the excavated evidence, the domestication of animals began in the Mesolithic period. The earliest pieces of evidence of domestication of animals in India have been found at Adamgarh (Narmadapuram, M.P.) and Bagor (Bhilwara, Rajasthan). *A large number of implements made of bones and horns have been found from the Mesolithic site, Mahadaha (located in Pratapgarh district of U.P.). The book titled 'Puratattva Vimarsh' written by Dr. Jai Narayan Pandey describes various pointed objects and ornaments made of bones which have been reported from Sarai Nahar Rai, Damdama and Mahadaha. *Damdama is a Mesolithic site in Pratapgarh district of Uttar Pradesh. I n Damdama, 41 human graves have been found. Out of these graves, 5 are double burials. One triple burial grave is also found here. A grave with four human skeletons has been found at Sarai Nahar Rai. *The Megaliths usually refer to the burials made up of large stones in graveyards away from the habitation area. A large fraction of these is assumed to be associated with burial or post-burial rituals including memorials for those whose remains may or may not be available. Some of these are; Chamber tomb, Dolmens, Stone alignment, Stone circle (cromlech), Pit-circles, etc. *According to 'Puratattva Vimarsh' by Dr. J.N. Pandey 17 human skeletons were found from rock shelter 1 of Lekhahiya in the Vindhya region. Some of these were in relatively pristine condition while most of the others were warped. *According to John R. Lucas of the University of Oregon (USA), remnants of 27 human skeletons were found in Lekhahiya. *The rock shelters of Bhimbetka are situated in the Raisen district of Madhya Pradesh. UNESCO has included the rock art of Bhimbetka in the list of its World Heritage Sites. These caves exhibit the earliest traces of human life on the Indian subcontinent and include pictures of an elephant, sambhar, deer, etc. *Grains were ﬁ rst ever produced in Neolithic Age. It was the time when people were introduced to agriculture. Koldihwa and Mehrgarh were the two Neolithic sites from where clear pieces evidence of rice and wheat have been found respectively. *There are mainly eight types of food grains consumed by modern human society, namely-barley, wheat, maize, millet, sorghum, mustard, oat and rice. These crops were present in the form of weeds in diﬀ erent areas, which were later grown as seeds by human beings at diﬀ erent places, at diﬀ erent times. *According to the latest research, the earliest evidence of agriculture in the Indian sub-continent was reported from the Lahuradewa site in Sant Kabir Nagar district, Uttar Pradesh. The evidence of human activity and beginning of rice cultivation at this site dates back to around 8000-7000 BC. *Signiﬁ cantly before this research, the earlier evidence of wheat was found at Mehrgarh (located in Balochistan, Pakistan) belonging to around 7000 BC and the earliest evidence of rice is known to be near the bank of the river Belan, district Prayagraj, from where rice bran was found dating back to 6500 BC. *The cultural remains from the Stone Age to Harappan Civilization have been found in Mehrgarh located in Balochistan (Pakistan). *The Burzahom site is a prehistoric settlement in the village of the same name in Kashmir valley. Both human and animal skeletons were found here with trepanning (bored holes) marks. In many pits, bones of dogs and antlered deer were found along with human skeletons. The skeletons of humans were found in the burial pits in a sitting position along with bones of animals. *The ﬁ rst excavation at the Burzahom site was carried out by Helmut de Terra and Dr. Thomas Paterson in 1935 A.D. *The people of Jorwe culture lived in large rectangular houses with wattle and daub walls and thatched roofs. They believed in life after death and therefore buried the dead inside the houses under the ﬂ oor. Children were buried in two urns that were joined mouth-to-mouth and set horizontally in the pit, while adults were placed in a supine position with their head towards the north (north to south). These sites were found in Daimabad, Inamgaon, Chandoli, Nevasa etc. *The ‘Ash mounds’ have been found from a Neolithic site Sangana Kallu located in Ballari district in Karnataka. They have also been found in Piklihal and Utnur. These ash mounds are the burnt relics of seasonal camps of Neolithic herdsmen community. *Fire was ﬁ rst used in the Neolithic period. *Copper was the ﬁ rst metal used. Copper Age is also known as the Chalcolithic Age . The age in which instruments of copper were used in addition to stone is called as Chalcolithic Age. *Settlements of Chalcolithic period in India were found in South-East Rajasthan, Western Madhya Pradesh, Western Maharashtra and South-East India. *Navdatoli has revealed excellent evidence of both round and rectangular residential structures which are located near Khargone district (M.P.). The former measures about 1-4.5 m in diameter and the latter is 5-6 m long *The roofs were probably made of hay, tree branches and leaves and were supported on massive wooden posts, 22cm in diameter, raised at regular intervals around the huts. *The open spaces between the posts were provided with mud-plastered bamboo screens. *The house ﬂ oors were made up of silt clay and river gravel, with the surface coated with lime. The huts were provided with one or two-mouthed ‘chulhas’ as well as storage jars and other earthen vessels. *Ochre-Coloured Pottery (known to archaeologists as OCP) as the name implies, its main distinguishing feature was when rubbed it left an ochre colour on ﬁ ngers. Other characteristics are its porous character and the fact that it is invariably wor n out at the edges. Most of its evidence is mainly found in Atranjikhera and Hastinapur. *The Archaeological Survey of India (ASI), under the Ministry of Culture, is a premier organization for the archaeological research and protection of the cultural heritage of the nation. In 1871 AD, the Archaeological Survey was established as a separate department and Alexander Cunningham was appointed as its ﬁ rst Director-General. In 1901 AD, during the tenure of Lord Curzon, it was centralized as Archaeological Survey of India and John Marshall assumed oﬃ ce in 1902 as its Director-General. *The National Museum of Mankind known as Indira Gandhi Rastriya Manav Sangrahalaya is located in Bhopal (M.P.). It is an autonomous organization under the Ministry of Culture.

title: Indus Valley Civilization
intro: Indian History General Studies B–17 Indus Valley Civilization The Indus Valley Civilization is also known as the Harappa Civilization. *Archaeologists use the term 'culture' for a group of objects, distinctive in style, that are usually found togeth er within a speciﬁ c geographical area and at a period of time. *In the case of Harappan culture, these distinctive objects include- seals, beads, weights, stone blades and even baked bricks. *The Harappan seal is possibly the most distinctive artefact of the Harappan or Indus Valley civilization. John Marshall, Director-General of the ASI, announced the discovery of a new civilization in the Indus Valley to the world in 1921. *Harappa is located in the Montgomery district (currently it is Sahiwal district) of Punjab province, Pakistan. *Mohenjodaro is located on the right bank of the Indus River in Larkana District of Sindh Province Pakistan. *According to Stuart Piggott, the two cities, Harappa and Mohenjodaro were “Twin capitals of one United Kingdom”. *Harappa is located at the left bank of Ravi River. *The carbon-14 (C 14) dating process indicates the Harappan period to be from 2600 BC to 1700 BC which is highly accepted. During the period 2300 BC to 1900 B.C., the growth of this civilization was at its peak. Mesopotamia and Egyptian civilization are contemporary to the Indus civilization. Bimbisara, the ruler of Magadha built a ‘Mahavihara’ called ‘Venuvana’ for his residence. *Travelling from Rajgriha, Buddha reached Vaishali, the capital of Lichchhavi where he spent the ﬁ fth year of the rainy season. *Lichchhivians built the famous ‘Kutagrasala’ in Mahavan for his residence. *Vaishali’s royal courtesan, Amrapali, became his disciple and provided his Amravatika for the residence of the Buddhist monks. *In the eighth year of Enlightenment, Gautama Buddha permitted women to enter as Bhikshuni into the Buddhist Sangha at Vaishali on the advice of his beloved disciple Ananda. *Buddha’s aunt (Mahaprajapati) who raised him as a mother was the ﬁ rst woman to enter the Buddhist Sangh. *Devadatta was the cousin of Buddha. *Devadatta ﬁ rst became a follower and then became an enemy of Buddha. *He wanted to remove Buddha from the Buddhist Sangh and become the head of the Sangh himself, but he did not succeed in it. The Buddhism was highly popularised in the Koshal state. *A wealthy businessman named Anathpindak of the Koshal kingdom became his disciple and donated him ‘Jetavana’ Vihara for the Buddhist Sangh. *Koshal King Prasenjit also adopted Buddhist religion along with his family. 'Pubharama' (Purva-Ram) vihara was built by Vishakha (disciple of Buddha) for buddhist sangh. *Buddha spent his last rainy season at Beluva village in Vaishali. *While preaching Buddhism, he reached Pava, where he stayed in the Amravatika of Chund, a blacksmith. *He gave Buddha ‘Sukaramaddava’ food to eat and this caused him ‘bleeding’. *Then he went to Kushinagar (Kushinara) and there he gave his last sermon to Subhadda. *He died in Kushinagar (capital of the Republic Malla) in 483 BC at the age of 80. In Buddhist texts, this event is called ‘Mahaparinirvana’. *Buddha’s first sermon is termed as ‘Dharmachakrap- ravartana’. The sermon was related to suﬀ ering, the cause of suﬀ ering and path leading to end of suﬀ ering. *The concept of eightfold path forms the theme of ‘Dharma Chakra Pravartana Sutta’, which means sermon of the turning of the wheel of law. He gave the ‘Noble Eightfold Path’ and ‘Four Noble Truths’, which were accepted as basic tenets by all Buddhist sects. *The four noble truths are as follows- i. There is suﬀ ering. ii. There is the cause of suﬀ ering. iii. There is a cessation of suﬀ ering. iv. There is a path leading to the cessation of suﬀ ering. One of the main reason for the spread of Buddhism was its simplicity. Its eightfold path and concept of non-violence were simple and understandable by the common people. Buddha spread his message in the simple language or the language of common people. *Buddhism did not believe in caste- distinctions. The non-Brahmins, particularly Lower-class were attracted by the simplicity of Buddhism. They also followed the missionary concept. Buddhist Councils Number Year Place President Rulers First 483 BC Rajgriha Mahakassapa or Mahakashyapa Ajatashatru Second 383 BC Vaishali Sabakami or Subukami Kalasoka Third 247 BC Pataliputra Moggaliputta Tissa Ashok Fourth 1 st Centu- ry AD Kundal- vana (Kashmir) Vasumitra Ashwaghosha (Vice President) Kanishka *In ﬁ rst century those who believed in traditional faith were called ‘Sthavira’ and later ‘Theravada’ . These were led by Mahakatyayana. *Those who accepted the change were called ‘Mahasanghika’. They were led by Mahakasappa. *In the fourth Buddhist council, there was a dominance of the Mahasanghikas. The fourth council, held during the reign of Kanishka, divided Buddhism into two sects, namely Hinayana and Mahayana. In Mahayana, Gautama Buddha was treated as God and its followers started worshipping Buddha through idols. Gautama Buddha was elevated to the position of God during the period of Kanishka. *The fundamental diﬀ erence between Hinayana and Mahayana sects of Buddhism is regard- ing treating Buddha as God. Hinayana believes in Buddha as a great man, whereas Mahayana started worshipping Buddha through idols treating him as God. *Sarvastivada literally means "Doctrine that all exist" . Sarvastivadin described a complex system in which past, present and future phenomena are all held to have some form of their own existence. *Like all Buddhist, the Sarvastivadins consider everything empirical to be transient but they maintain that the dharma factors are eternally existing realities. *Impermanence, also called Anitya, is one of the essential doctrines and part of three marks of existence in Buddhism. This doctrine was presented by Buddha himself. The doctrine asserts that all of conditioned existence, without exception, is "transient, evanescent, inconstant". This impermanence is a source of Dukkha (suﬀ erings). *Nagarjuna’s primary contribution to Buddhist philosophy was the use of the concept of Sunyata or doctrine of void. *The famous literary work “Madhyamikakarika” provides one of Nagarjuna’s most famous quotations on emptiness or co-arising. Nagarjuna was an eminent personality in the court of Kanishka. *Hiuen Tsang called him one of the world's four great guiding powers. *In the book "Madyamikakarika" he has discussed the theory of relativity . He is also known as the Indian Einstein. According to Chinese mythology, Nagarjuna travelled to China and preached Buddhism. *‘Maitreya’ has been called ‘future Buddha’ in Buddhist tradition. *“Padma- pani or “Lotus-Bearer” is one of the most common epithets of Avalokiteshvara, the Bodhisattva of inﬁ nite compassion. This superbly modelled sculpture stands in a tribhanga or tri-bent pose. *A Bodhisattva is a living being (sattva) who aspires to enlightenment (bodhi) and carries out altruistic practices. The Bodhisattva ideal is central to the Mahayana Buddhist tradition as the individual who seeks enlightenment both for himself or herself and for others. *In order to preach the doctrine of Buddhism (Mahatma Bud- dha), the Buddhists compiled a new type of literature (Tripitaka) that can be divided into three categories - (1) Sutta Pitaka, (2) Vinaya Pitaka and (3) Abhidhamma Pitaka. * Sutta Pitaka contains the sayings and teachings of the Buddha. * Vinaya Pitaka deals with the rules to be observed by members of the Sangha. Abhidhamma Pitaka presents the philosophical ex- position of the Dhamma. The Abhidhamma Pitaka consists of seven books - Yamaka, Patthana, Kathavatthu, Puggalapannatti, Dhatukatha, Vibhanga and Dhammasangani. *The religious texts of the Buddhists, in which the stories of the previous birth of Gautama Buddha are compiled, are called Jataka. They were kept alive orally before being written in pali language. *In Bhumisparsha Mudra, Buddha is seen seated with his right hand as a pendant over the right knee reaching towards the ground with the palm inward while touching the lotus throne. and left hand rests in his lap, palm facing upward. This gesture represents the moment of the Buddha's awakening as he claims the earth as the witness of his enlightenment just before he real- ized enlightenment. It is believed that the demon Mara tried to frighten him with the armies of demons which represent the defeat of Mara and his demonic army by Buddha. *During the Gupta and post-gupta period, some of the most im- portant centres of learning in India were Nalanda, Vikramshila and Vallabhi. These centers of learning were not only popular among the diﬀ erent Janapadas from where students came for learning but also attracted students from abroad i.e. China, Japan, Tibet and other countries of South-East Asia. *Some of the educational centers like Taxila and Nalanda were major centre of learning. *Nalanda was the main centre for the edu- cation of Mahayana Buddhism and Vallabhi for Hinayana Buddhism. * Vikramshila Mahavihara was established by Pala King Dharmapala . *He also constructed temples and monasteries here. *The University of Nalanda came into exis- tence during the Gupta Period. *Initially Kumaragupta - I gave donations to Nalanda Buddhist Vihara and afterwards Buddhgupta, Tathagatgupta and Baladitya also donated to this Vihara. *“Navnalanda Mahavihara” is a modern centre of Buddhist study. Its foundation stone was laid on 20 November 1951. *Odantapuri (also called as Uddantapura) was a prominent education centre of ancient times. It was situated in Magadha, now Bihar, India. It was established by the Pala emperor Gopala I. *“Chaitya” literally means - related to (funeral pyre) i.e. Chita. *Samadhis were built on the ground after the burial of dead bodies, they were initially called Chaitya or Stupa. * In these samadhis, residues of great men were kept safe, therefore Chaityas became a centre of worship. *The houses built near monasteries or Chaitya Griha were called Vihara. *The word stupa has been used for the ﬁ rst time in Rig Veda. In Rig Veda texts, stupa means “tree stem.” Rigveda refers to a stupa raised by the king Varuna above the forest in a place having no foundation. Anything that is raised on the ground like a heap/ pile might have been known as Stupa. Mahabodhi Temple at Bodhgaya is related to the enlighten- ment of Buddha. Sanchi Stupa is not related to any episode of Buddha’s life. *In these stupas the remains of Buddha or his chief disciples were kept, so they became the main centres of devotion and worship of the Buddhists. * Stupa has 4 types - 1. Sharirik (Body) Stupa, 2. Paribhogika Stupa, 3. Uddheshika (Objective) Stupas and 4. Vratanusthit (Worshipping) Stupa. *Gautama Buddha is known as ‘ Light of Asia’. The book ‘The Light of Asia’ on the life of Gautama Buddha was writ- ten by Edwin Arnold. Mahaparinirvana temple is located in Kushinagar district of Uttar Pradesh. Statue of Lord Buddha in the temple was obtained by excavation in 1876-77 AD. It is 6.10 meters high in this temple and is placed in a lying pose. *This idol reﬂ ects the period when Lord Buddha at the age of 80 left his earthly body and became free from the bondage of death i.e Parinirvana. title: Gupta and Post-Gupta Period
intro: Gupta and Post-Gupta Period *Gupta dynasty ruled during 275-550 AD. This dynasty was established by King Srigupta around 275 AD, but the ﬁ rst powerful ruler of Gupta dynasty was Chandragupta I who ruled during 319-335 AD . He held the title of ‘Maharajadhiraja’ (in contradiction to his predecessors) to show his importance. * Gupta Samvat was started by Chandragupta-I in 319 A.D. *Historian V . A. Smith in his composition ‘The Early History of India’ called Samudragupta (335-375 A.D.) of Gupta dynasty as ‘Napoleon of India’ for his great military conquests. The Allahabad (Prayag) stone/pillar inscription of Samudragupta, engraved on an Ashoka pillar at Allahabad (Prayagraj) is associated with Samudragupta (335-375 AD). It is considered to be the most important historical document of the classical Gupta age in Sanskrit written by Harisena. It is also known as ‘Prayag Prashasti’. *The inscription is a panegyric (tribute) praising Samudragupta and lists the political and military achievements of his reign including his expeditions to the south. Built by Ashoka, originally it was situated in Kaushambi, which was later shifted to Allahabad (Prayagraj) by Akbar. The name of Jahangir and Birbal is also mentioned there. *Prayag Prashasti is on the Ashokan Pillar but has 4 diﬀ erent inscriptions: (1) Ashokan inscription in Brahmi script (2) Queen edict regarding the charitable deed of Ashoka’s wife, Karuvaki. (3) Samudragupta inscription written by Harisena in Sanskrit language and Brahmi script. (4) Jahangir inscription in Persian. *Another name of Gupta ruler Chandragupta –II ‘Vikramaditya’ (375-415 AD) is found as Devgupta. Its evidence has been obtained from Sanchi and Vakataka inscriptions. Apart from the above-mentioned names, he is also known as Devraja (Sanchi inscription) and Devashri. *According to Mehrauli inscription the king Chandra was devoted to Vishnu and set up the Vishnu dhvaja (in honour of the God Vishnu) on a hill called Vishnupada. *‘Mehrauli Iron Pillar Inscription’ acquired from Mehrauli in Delhi is located in the centre of the courtyard of Quwwat-ul-islam mosque near Qutub Minar at present. *Gupta ruler Chandragupta-II ‘Vikramaditya’ was known as the ‘Saka Conqueror’ as he admonished Saka power by defeating last Saka king of western India Rudrasimha-III. He adopted the title of ‘Sakari’ after this victory. He launched silver coins on this occasion. They were called ‘Rupaka’ in Gupta rule. The Nine Gems of Chandragupta II were (1) Kalidas (Poet), (2) Dhanvantari (Physician), (3) Varahamihira (Astronomer), (4) Amar Simha (Lexicographer), (5) Shanku (Architect) (6) Kshapanak (Astrologer), (7) Vararuchi (Grammarian), (8) Vetala Bhatta (Magician) (9) Ghata Karpara (Diplomat). *Kumaragupta I ‘ Mahendraditya’ ( 415-455 AD) was the son born to Dhruvadevi, wife of Chandragupta II. *The ﬁ rst invasion of Hunas took place during the reign of Skandagupta (455-467 AD) and Hunas were comprehensively defeated by him. This invasion was just like a raid without any lasting impact on India, but this invasion hastened the decline of the Gupta Empire. Hunas annexed many regions of the north-west in the transition period of 5th-6th centuries after the death of Skandagupta. *Bhitari Pillar inscription is found from a place named Bhitari in Saidpur tehsil of district Ghazipur, Uttar Pradesh. The description of the war between Skandagupta and Hunas is mentioned in Bhitari Pillar inscription. It is noteworthy that the ﬁ rst Indian invasion of Hunas took place during the reign of Skandagupta (455-467 AD) in which Hunas were badly defeated by Skandagupta. When the Hunas invasion ended the Roman Empire in 3rd century AD., the Indian merchants relied more and more on the South East Asian trade. *Toramana was the leader of the second Hunas attack on India. *Mihirakula was a central Asian Hunas origin, who was one of the most important Hephthalite Emperor. The Gwalior inscription showed his territory which included Gwalior. Mihirakula suﬀ ered a defeat by the Aulikara king Yasodharman of Malwa in 528 AD. or by some other sources 495 A.D. *The Tamralipti port in Bengal was a prominent port during Gupta period from where trade was conducted with south-east Asia, China, Lanka, Java, Sumatra as well as northern India. Western coast had an important port of BhriguKachchha (Bharuch) from where Gupta rulers used to trade with western countries. *Guilds were very important in the economy of ancient India. These organizations were established by merchants for the proper regulation of their trade. Guilds had the judicial power of their members and also had the power to ensure the salary, rules of job, standards and prices. Every guild had its head without any intervention by the kingdom but operated under royal recognition. It was also important for governing the local bodies. *Gujarat, Bengal, Deccan and Tamil Nadu were famous for the production of the garments in the Gupta period. The textile industry was the principal industry of the Gupta period. During the Gupta period, the main centres of international trade were Tamralipti, Bhrigu Kachchha, Arikamedu, Kaveripattanam, Muziris, Pratishthana, Sopara, Barberikam. *Dhanvantari was one of the Navratnas of Chandragupta II. He was a master in Ayurveda. Bhaskara I was Post-Gupta contemporary. He wrote Mahabhaskariya & Laghubhaskariya. Bhaskaracharya (Bhaskara II)was a great astronomer and mathematician. He composed ‘Siddhanta Shiromani’ and ‘Lilavati’ based on astronomy and mathematics. He was not a contemporary of Guptas. He belonged to 12th century. *Development in mathematics is notable in the Gupta period. Indian History General Studies B–131 Sine, Cosine, and Inverse sine were known in 5 th Century. These are mentioned in ‘Surya Siddhanta’ and ‘Aryabhatiya’. Brahmagupta described cyclic quadrilateral. We find six types of gold currencies during the reign of Samudragupta. They were Garuda, Archer, Parashu, Ashvamedha, Vaghra- Prakramah, Veena Type. According to the Chinese traveller Fa-Hien, people used Cowrie shells in routine trading activities. Coins of Gupta rulers were found in Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Bengal, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, Orissa (Odisha). The most famous place where coins were found in Bayana (Bharatpur, Rajasthan). Silver Coins issued by them were known as Rupaka and the gold coins were called Dinara. *The ﬁ rst inscriptional evidence of ‘Sati Practice’ in India is mentioned in the Eran inscription. This inscription belongs to 510 AD in which the practice of Sati was mentioned for a lady who was the wife of a war commander named Goparaja. *During Gupta period, towns declined gradually. All the towns which were prosperous in the valley, most of them had declined in that age. A major city, Pataliputra was in ruins with a smaller inhabited settlement remained when Hiuen-Tsang came to India. Mathura, Sonpur, Hastinapur, Sravasti etc., all major cities provided evidence of a decline in this age. *Gupta period in ancient India is considered as the golden age due to the excellent development in the ﬁ eld of art and culture. *The ruler of Gupta dynasty donated the maximum number of villages to temples and Brahmins. Also, the income generated from the land of the village used to be given to the owner of the land. A person who used to cultivate on the oﬃ cial land of the ruler had to pay a part of crop-products as tax in the Gupta period which was the sixth portion (1/6) of the production. *Land revenue is known as ‘Udranga’ and “Bhag” in Gupta inscriptions. *In ancient India, the irrigation tax was known as ‘Udakabhog.’ * Hiranya was the cash tax in Mauryan period. The land tax was called Udranga in Gupta inscriptions. Uparikara was tax imposed on farmers without any proprietary rights in the soil, a tax on temporary tenants, or an additiona l cess. *In Sanskrit plays, written during Gupta period, women and Sudras spoke in Prakrit dialects while upper varnas (classes) used Sanskrit to speak. *Except for Vedic age, the situation of women was never good in ancient India. In the age of Gupta, Maurya and Chola, the evidence of inferior status of women has been found. Thus, situation of women with men cannot be compared in any age. ‘Mrichchhakatika’ written by Shudraka oﬀ ers a picture of urban social life and politics in its dramatic setting during the Gupta period. This text deals with the love story of Charudatta, a rich merchant with the Vasantasena, the daughter of a courtesan. *The rule of the Gupta Empire was monarchical. Unlike other rulers, the Gupta rulers believed in their divine origin. The Gupta rulers expanded the tradition of donation of land. The nature of the Gupta administration was not centralized and conservative; the Gupta king was the king of many smaller kingdoms. The feudal and provincial rulers experienced absolute independence in their respective areas. *The game of chess originated in India during Gupta period, known as ‘Chaturanga.’ It reached Iran and then Europe from India. Pravarasena I (275-335 AD) the ruler of Vakataka dynasty, was the ﬁ rst Vakataka ruler who called himself a Samrat. Vakataka ruler Pravarasena I conducted four Ashvamedha Yajnas. Along with this, he also made many Vedic sacriﬁ ces. Emperor Pravarasena II of the same dynasty was interested in literature; he composed a treatise called ‘Setubandha’. *Hindu philosophy refers to a group of darshans (philosophies, worldviews, teachings) that emerged in ancient India. The mainstream Hindu philosophy includes six systems (Saddarsana) Sankhya, Yoga, Nyaya, Vaisheshika, Mimamsa, and Vedanta. *Sankhya Darshan is one of the most ancient philosophical schools of India. Maharshi Kapila is known as the ‘Acharya’ of Sankhya Darshan. ‘Sankhya Sutra’ and Tattva samas (late 14th-15th century text of uncertain author) are traditionally attributed to Kapila. *Sankhya philosophy accepts the theory of rebirth or transmigration of the soul . Nescience is the cause of sorrow and self-enlightenment through knowledge is the solution for liberation from it. Sankhya held that it is th e self-knowledge that leads to liberation and not any exterior inﬂ uence or agent. *Maharshi Patanjali is known as the founder of ‘Yoga Darshan.’ The description of yoga is found in Upanishad, Mahabharat, Bhagavad Geeta, Jain and Buddha texts. Maharshi Patanjali explained it as a compact philosophical theory. So it is called as 'Patanjali Darshan’. Ashtanga Yoga means “eight- limbed yoga” as outlined by the sage Patanjali in the Yog Sutras. It consists of eight spiritual practices. Yama, Niyama, Asana, Pranayama, Pratyahara, Dharana, Dhyana and Samadhi. Patanjali was contemporary to Pushyamitra Shunga (184-148 BC). *‘Nyaya Darshan’ was propagated by Gautama who is also known as ‘Akshapada’. The word ‘Nyaya’ means decision or logics . Nyaya Darshan recognizes the existence of 16 substances or logics. The original text of Nyaya Darshan is ‘Nyayasutra’ which is the masterpiece of Gautama. *The theory of karma is related to ‘Mimamsa’ philosophy. It is also known as Karma Mimamsa, Purva Mimamsa or Dharma Mimamsa. *‘Mimamsa’ philosophy accepts that Vedas contain the eternal truth. Purva Mimamsa tells about ‘Karmakanda’ while Uttar Mimamsa tells about ‘Gyankand’. *Vedanta philosophy is considered to be one of the six (systems) darshans of Indian philosophy (often treated as culmination of Vedic thought). Vedanta literally means - ‘The end of the Vedas’ or ‘the climax of Vedic ideology’. Vedanta philosophy has three bases - Upanishads, Brahmasutra and Bhagavad Gita. They are called the ‘Prasthanatrayi’. *Maharshi Kanad was the founder of Vaisheshika School of Indian philosophy. He propounded atom theory and is called the founder of Indian Atomism. According to this theory material, subjects are made up of atoms. The Vaisheshika thus marked the beginning of physics in India. Kanad was ﬁ rst to prove that atom is the smallest unit of any matter. Atom cannot be seen through naked eyes and cannot be further divided. *The Vaisheshika school gives importance to the discussion of substance or dravya. Earth, Water, Fire, Air and Sky, when combine give rise to new objects. *According to Puranas, Chandravansh (or Somvansha) was one of the prime dynasties of the Kshatriya varna. The prime place of the Chandravansha’s ruler was Prayag but after a natural calamity, Dwapar Yug Chandravanshi king Samvaram established his capital in Pratishthanpur (present Jhunsi, Prayagraj). *Pratihara dynasty was one of the most famous agnikula clan. It is known as the Gurjara- Pratihara dynasty in history as evidenced from epigraphic-historical usage. *The ﬁ rst description of the Gurjara caste is in the Aihole text of Pulakeshin II. Gurjars are mentioned in the Harshacharita of Banabhatta. The founder of the Gurjara-Pratihara dynasty was Nagabhata I (730 - 756 AD). The Gwalior inscription shows that he had destroyed the large army of Mlechcha king, which was probably the Arab ruler of Sindh according to some historians. *The Rashtrakuta dynasty was established in 753 A.D. by Dantidurga. He made the Manyakheta as his capital. About Dantidurga, it is said that in Ujjaini, he conducted a Hiranyagarbha (Mahadan) Yajna. *Rashtrakuta ruler Amoghavarsha I was born in 800 AD in the military camp of Sribhavan, on the banks of river Narmada. At this time, his father, Rashtrakuta King Govind III was returning after successful campaigns of North India. Maukhari were the feudatories of the Guptas, who were originally residents of Gaya. The rulers of the Maukhari dynasty made Kannauj their capital. Hari Varma, Aditya Varma, Ishvara- Varma, Sharva-Varma and Graha-Varma were the main rulers of this dynasty. *Detailed information regarding Harsha is obtained from Harshacharita, which was composed by author Banabhatta. Some information regarding him is also available from Rajatarangini written by Kalhana. *Chinese sources revealed that Harsha and Rajyashri ruled together over Kannauj. Harsha shifted his capital to Kannauj from Thaneshwar to help his sister Rajyashri in the proper administration of Kannauj. Harsha held a massive council of various religions and sects in Kannauj. According to the Chinese evidence, rulers of 20 countries along with their eminent Brahmins, shramanas, courtiers, etc. arrived there. This meeting was presided over by Harsha Vardhana. A function used to be held at Sangam region of Prayagraj every ﬁ fth year of Harsha’s rule, which is stated as ‘Mahamoksha council.’ Hiuen Tsang himself attended the 6th function which was attended by 18 rulers of various countries. *Emperor Harsha’s southward march was stopped on the Narmada River by Pulakesin-II. Pulakesin-II also wanted to expand the state towards the north, in such a situation the war was inevitable between the two. Actually, there was a war between the two, at the bank of the Narmada, in which Pulakesin-II defeated Harsha. This incident is mentioned in Aihole inscription of Pulakesin-II and description of Hiuen Tsang. *The arrival of Hiuen Tsang was the most important event of Harsha’s period. He departed for India in 629 AD from Changan, the capital of Tang ruler. He wrote a book on his tour to India named 'Sei-Yu-Kei'. *Hiuen Tsang went to Nalanda University in 637 AD. Acharya Sheelbhadra was the vice-chancellor of Nalanda University at that time. According to Hiuen Tsang, Mathura was famous for the production of cotton textiles at that time, while, Varanasi was famous for the silk textiles. Hiuen Tsang says that the main reason for the prosperity of Thaneshwar was the trade there. *Kannauj became the center of attraction for various powers after Harsha’s death. It has been expressed by the names ‘Mahodaya’, ‘Mahodayashri’ etc. There was a triangular struggle between the three great powers of the 8th century- Pala, Gurjara-Pratihara and Rashtrakuta for the control of Kannauj which is the most important event in the history of North India in the 8 th-9th century. In this struggle, ultimately, the Pratiharas got success. *The Chinese traveller Itsing with 37 Buddhist associates decided to travel to western countries in 671 or 672 AD. He came to India through southern sea route at Tamralipti and returned to China in 693 - 94 AD via Sumatra. In ancient days, Chinese writers mentioned India by the names of ‘Yin-tu’ and ‘Thian-tu’. Nalanda University was ransacked and destroyed by the army of Bakhtiyar Khalji in the end of 12th century A.D. (around 1193 A.D.). It was the ﬁ nal blow to Buddhism in India and set it on the path of decline. *Shankaracharya is also known as Shankar, Shree Shankaracharya etc. He was born in Kaladi, a small village in Kerala in the 8th century. His philosophy is known as ‘Advaita Vedanta’. The religious centres established by him are – (1) Sringeri (Karnataka) in south, (2) Dwarka (Gujarat) in west, (3) Puri (Odisha) – in the east and (4) Jyotirmath (Joshimath, Uttarakhand) - in the north. Badrinath, Dwarka, Puri and Rameswaram are Chardham, while Gangotri, Yamunotri, Kedarnath and Badrinath are the Chota (lesser) Dhaam located in Uttarakhand.

title: South India (Chola, Chalukya, Pallava and Sangam Period)
intro: South India (Chola, Chalukya, Pallava and Sangam Period) *According to the Sangam text, the terms Kon, Ko and Mannan were attributed to the King. Sangam is deﬁ ned as ‘Conference of Poets’ or ‘Forum of Scholars.’ Literature written by scholars during this conference, the oldest in south India, consisting of several collections or anthologies of poems, is mentioned as ‘Sangam Literature.’ *Three Sangams were held under the patronage of Pandya kings in the south. Sangam Place President First Madurai Saint Agastya and T olkappiyar Second Kapadapuram Saint Agastya Third Madurai Nakkirara *Agastya was the sage who is credited with having Aryanised south India. He was born in Kashi, and it is believed that he travelled south from Kashi on request of Gods and later resided in the south. He is also known as “Father of Tamil Literature.” Tolkappiyam is not only the residual text of 2nd Sangam era but also most ancient available text of Tamil literature. Author Tolkappiyar was one among the 12 disciples of Saint Agastya. It is a treatise on grammar and poetry. It has been written in formula style. *The author of Tamil Literature Silappadikaram was Ilango Adigal, second son of famous king Nedun-ceraladan of the Chera dynasty The epic narrates the tragic and poignant story of Kannagi and her husband, Kovalan. *Kural is considered as the Ethical bible of Tamil and Laghuveda of Tamil literature. It is also known as ‘Muppal’. It was written by the famous poet Tiruvalluvar. *Ramavataram, which is Tamil Ramayanam was authored by Kamban. *The history of early Cholas of Sangam literature, is the interregnum between fall of Sangam Chola and the rise of Medieval Chola under Vijayalaya (850-871 AD.) in the 9 th century. *Chola dynasty was established by Vijayalaya-I in Southern India. Parantaka - I defeated Madura/Pandya king Rajasimha and assumed the title of “Madurai-Kond.” *Rajaraja-I defeated Cheras naval army in Kandalloor and his son Rajendra-I sent an expedition against Sailendra empire of South East Asia and conquered some of the areas as they were facing diﬃ culty in trade with China. *A special feature of the Chola dynasty was the autonomy of village administration . The Chola village administration was very systematic and well-developed. In fact, the autonomous administration was implemented in the village during the Chola era. *A detailed description of the working system of the executive committee of Gram Sabha (village assembly) in Chola village administration has been archived from Uttaramerur inscription , which states that every village had its own committee called 'Sabha', which was usually independent of Central command and independently administered the village administration. *A working committee that supervised the activities of Chola-era villages was known as Variyam. * Thotta Variyam looked after Horticulture Board (garden administration) while Samvatsara Variyam was annual committee; Eri Variyam was in charge of tanks (lakes) and water supply and Pon Variyam was related to gold/ﬁ nance committee. *Brihadeeswara temple is an excellent piece of Dravidian style temple of Chola-style, which was constructed in the reign of Rajaraja-I. It is considered the largest and tallest temple in India. *There are idols of ‘Dwarpals’ around the main shrine. A gigantic 'Nandi' (carved out of a single rock) is situated in the exterior of sacrarium which is believed to be the talles t Nandi idol in India. *Chola Kings maintained a powerful standing army and a powerful navy. The Chola navy played a vital role in the expansion of the Chola Empire including the conquests of Ceylon (Sri Lanka) islands and naval raids on Srivijaya, Sinhala and Maldives. *The golden era of Chola empire started with the accession of Rajaraja- I to the throne. Rajaraja- I was the ﬁ rst Chola king who created Naval Army. * Rajendra Chola-I was a Chola emperor, who is considered as one of the greatest rulers and military generals of India. He succeeded his father, Rajaraja Chola-I. *Rajendra-I conquered the Sri Lanka and brought the king of Sinhaldweep (Sri Lanka) Mahinda-V to Chola kingdom as prisoner. He also defeated Pala ruler Mahipala and adopted the title of Gangaikonda Chola. Rajendra-I founded a new capital called Gangaikonda Cholapuram. The Chola navy was the strongest in the area, and they converted the Bay of Bengal into Chola lake. * Chola Gangam Ponneri was an artiﬁ cial lake constructed by Chola king Rajendra Chola-I in memory of his victory over rulers of Ganga river basin, including Bengal Kings and Kalinga Dynasty. *Vijayabahu, the Ceylon king, proclaimed independent Sinhala Island during the period of Kulottunga-I, but Kulottunga did not show any incivility and married his daughter to Sinhala prince Virapperumal. *Generally, Chola emperors used to elect their ‘Yuvraj” during their tenure, who becomes the heir of Empire after them. *Sangam literature describes the emergence and development of Chola, Chera and Pandya rulers. *During the reign of Chola ruler Kulottunga-I, 1077 AD, a Chola Buddhist delegation of 72 merchants was sent to China. *The Chola empire was divided into six provinces for the convenience of administration. *The provinces were called ‘Mandalam’. *A province was divided into ‘Kottam’ or ‘Valanadu’. *It was like the commissionerates. There were many ‘Nadu’ in each Kottam. *The district was called ‘Nadu’. *The assembly of Nadu was called ‘Nattar’. Indian History General Studies B–171 *The village association was called ‘Kurram’. *The smallest unit of administration was Gram Sabha. Chola artists were accomplished in carving art. *They created/carved stones and metals. They also prepared bronze sculptures more than stone sculptures. Most elegant idols of Nataraja (Shiva) are found in large numbers. They are included among best sculptures of the world. These images show Shiva with four arms. *The Dakshinamurti idol of Shiva depicts him as a mentor (Guru, Teacher) . Shiva is considered in this form as providing knowledge to his devotees. Dakshinamurti idol is installed facing south direction. *The battle of Takkolam was a military engagement between Rajaditya, son of the Chola king Parantaka - I and a confederacy of western Gangas, Banas and Vaidunbas led by Rashtrakuta King Krishna - III at Takkolam. The battle fought in 949 AD resulted in the defeat of Cholas and the death of Rajaditya on the battleﬁ eld. *Pallava ruler Simhavishnu (575-600 AD) assumed the titles of Avanisimha. *He defeated the kings of Chola, Pandya, Singhal and Kalmra. * Narasimhavarman I (630 - 668 AD) assumed the title of ‘Mahamalla’. *Parmeshwara Varman I (670-700 AD) assumed the title of Lokaditya, Ekmalla, Ranajaya, Atyantakama, Ugradanda, Gunabhajana etc. *Mahendravarman-I (600-630 AD) composed a humourous book titled ‘Mattvilasaprahasan’. The list of various ports is available in ‘Periplus of the Erythraean Sea", the famous book of an anonymous Greek sailor. Tondi, Mushiri and Nelisanda were the main ports of the western coast. At present, the ancient city of Vatapi is in Bagalkot district (Karnataka) named Badami. It was the second capital of Chalukyas during the 6th -7th century. Pulakesin - I was the real founder of Vatapi’s Chalukya dynasty. Women were appointed to high designations in Chalukya administration. *Vijaya Bhattarika, the Queen of Chandraditya (brother of Vikramaditya - I), issued two copper plates by her name. She was an excellent poetess too. Vijayaditya granted a village to a Jain Monastery on the recommendation of his younger sister Kumkumdevi. Vijaya Bhattarika ran the administration after her husband Chandraditya's death. * Pulakesin - II was the most capable and powerful ruler of Chalukyas, who ruled from 610 to 642 AD. Aihole inscription provides the saga of his achievements. *Ma-twa-lin was a Chinese traveller who has given an account of the relationship between China and India during the reign of Chalukyas. *Indian black pepper was a favourite ingredient of the most expensive Roman cookery. In Europe, the ﬁ rst spice that was used was pepper, and it gained an enormous social and economic value there. Greeks were familiar with the use of black pepper as early as 4th century BC, though it was probably an uncommon and expensive item. That is why in Sanskrit it is called as ‘Yavanapriya’ (dear to Yavanas/Greeks). Arikamedu is an archaeological site in southern India at Pondicherry. An intaglio was found here, which was carved with the picture of a man. It was identiﬁ ed as Augustus Caesar of Roman Empire. Beads and gems were also found. These ﬁ ndings indicate Indo- Roman trade contacts/Roman-world connections. Dubreuil called Arikamedu “a true Roman city.” In Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, it was called as Poduke. *Amphora Jar is an ancient jar with a long and narrow neck and two handles, one on either side. This jar was used in ancient Rome as a container for wine or oil. *Various trade unions/merchant guilds existed in South India like Manigramam, Nanadesi, Valanjiyar, etc. The purpose of these unions was to encourage trade and business. *Uraiyur was a very signiﬁ cant town during Sangam Era, located on the bank of Cauvery River in Tiruchirappalli (Tamil Nadu). It was known as Koli and Varanam and was the major center of cotton. It is mentioned in “Periplus of the Erythraen. Sea” as Argaru Vaigai River was the lifeline of the state of Pandya. The river originates in Varushanadu hills near Madurai, Tamil Nadu. Pandya state was located to the south of Cauvery. It comprises the districts of modern Madurai and some regions of Travancore also. Its capital was Madura. *Chera was a state of South India located in the present-day state of Kerala and to a lesser extent, parts of Tamil Nadu. The capital of the state of Chera was Vanchi. *The capital of Kadamba rulers was Banavasi (also known as Vaijayanti). Kadamba dynasty was founded by Mayurasharman. The Kadamb a state was annexed by Pulakesin - II. *Pandya king of South India sent an ambassador to the kingdom of Rome in 26 B.C. Pandya dynasty had the longest duration of reign in South Indian region (almost 200 BC to 1378 A.D.). Their capital was Korkai (early phase) and Madurai (later). *Meenakshi temple was originally built by Kulasekara Pandya. It is located in Madurai, and the lotus-shaped city surrounds it completely.

title: Muslim Invasion of India
intro: Muslim Invasion of India *Mecca is situated in Saudi Arabia. The propounder of Islam religion, Hazarat Muhammad, was born here in 570 A.D. The place is a religious pilgrimage for Islamic followers. Muhammad died in 632 A.D. *Rigveda mentions the Bharatas as a tribe/people. The land name Bharat/Bharatavarsa is stated in later sanskrit texts (e.g. Vishnu Purana). According to tradition, the country was named after Dushyanta's son, 'Bharat'. *According to some scholars, the country is named after the name of Rishabhanath’s eldest son 'Bharat'. *Iranians addressed this country as ‘Hindustan’, and Greeks called it ‘India’. With respect to the people of Hind (Bharat), the word ‘Hindu’ was ﬁ rst used by Iranian/Persian. *The ﬁ rst successful Muslim invasion of India took place in 712 AD under the leadership of Arabian invader “Muhammad-Bin Qasim’. Earlier before 712 AD, a campaign was undertaken to India under the leadership of Ubaidullah, but he was defeated and killed in the encounter. After a great struggle Arabians conquered Sindh in 712 AD. Sindh was ruled by Dahir at that time. According to Persian texts ‘Chachnama’ we came to know about the conquest of Sindh by Arabians. Note: The year of the ﬁ rst successful invasion of India by Muslims is a subject of dispute among scholars. According to V .D. Mahajan, it is dated in 711 A.D. whereas according to Harishchandra Verma, it took place in 712 A.D. *The founder of Ghaznavid Empire was Alptigin. Ghaznavid dynasty is also known as Yamini dynasty. Alptigin made Ghazni his capital. In 998 AD, Mahmud became the ruler of Ghazni. According to Sir Henry Elliot, Mahmud invaded India 17 times. Mahmud Ghaznavi plundered Somnath Temple during the reign of Bhimdev I (1022-63). *Mahmud Ghaznavi, for the ﬁ rst time, invaded Chandelas in 1019-20 AD. At that time, the ruler of Chandela dynasty was Vidyadhar, who was the most powerful ruler of the dynasty. He was a Hindu ruler who had successfully resisted Muslim invasions. Between 1000-1027 AD, Mahmud Ghazni (Ghaznavi) attacked India 17 times, but the motive of these invasions was not to establish a stable Muslim rule in India but only to plunder the material assets. Baghdad’s Caliph Al- Qadir-Billah titled Mahmud Ghaznavi as ‘Yamin-ud-Daula’ and ‘Amin-ul-Millah’. II. Medieval History of India *Mahmud Ghaznavi patronised Persian learning. He respected scholars and artists alongwith famous scholars in Ghazni at that time. Utbi was his court historian. He wrote texts like Al-Kitab- al-Yamini/ ‘Tarikh-i-Yamini’. Other prominent members of his court were Albiruni, Baihaqi (writer of Tarikh-i-Subuktigin), Persian poet Uzari and Unsuri, Asjadi and Farrukhi. *The author of Shahnama is Firdausi. He was a famous court poet of Mahmud Ghaznavi. He earned the titled of ‘Homer of the East’. Firishta (1560-1620 A.D.) wrote books like Tarikh-i- Firishta, also Known as Gulshan-i- Ibrahimi. His full name was Muhammad Qasim Hindu Shah Astarabadi Firishta. His book ‘Tarikh-i-Firishta’ is dedicated to the ruler of Bijapur Ibrahim Adil Shah II. In the 11 th century, Al-Biruni came to India with Mahmud Ghazanavi. From his book ‘Kitab-ul-hind’ we come to know about the social and cultural conditions of contemporary India. *Al-Biruni was the ﬁ rst Muslim to study Puranas. He was born in 973 AD and was a resident of Khiva (ancient Khwarizm). He came to India with Mahmud Ghaznavi. Al-Biruni was not only a historian, his knowledge and interest included Astronomy, Geography, logic, medicine, mathematics, religion and theology. He studied Sanskrit, including many literary works of Brahmagupta, Balabhadra and Varahmihira are outlined especially. Al-Biruni wrote ‘Tahqiq-i-Hind’ in the Arabic language. * Edward Sachau translated this text from Arabic into English language. It was translated into Hindi by Rajnikant Sharma. Mahmud Ghazanavi introduced silver coins with Sanskrit legend. The two sides of the silver coin were marked with the legend in two diﬀ erent languages. The legend on the upper side was inscribed in the Arabic language, and the other side was inscribed in the Sanskrit language (Sharada Script). In the middle part of the coin was written in Sanskrit language - “Avyaktmekam Muhammad Avatar Nripati Mahmud”. *Ghurid ruler from Ghor (present day Afghanistan) Shihabuddin Muhammad Ghori ﬁ rst invaded India in 1175 AD. In 1178 AD, Muhammad Ghori invaded Gujarat, but Mularaja-II or Bhimdev-II, under the leadership of his qualiﬁ ed and courageous widowed mother Naika Devi fought and defeated Ghori near Mount Abu. It was the ﬁ rst defeat of Ghori in India. *In 1191 AD, Prithviraj Chauhan and Ghori fought the ﬁ rst battle of Tarain. In 1192 AD, Muhammad Ghori defeated Prithviraj Chauhan in the second battle of Tarain, and laid the foundation of Muslim power in India. Ghori’s alertness and skilled battle techniques were the main factors in the victory of the Muslims. Prithviraj Chauhan while trying to escape, was caught near Sursati (modern Sirsa, Haryana). *For the death of Prithviraj Chauhan diﬀ erent opinions were given, but among those opinions, the opinion of Hasan Nizami is widely accepted, which says that Prithviraj's son was appointed to govern Ajmer when Prithviraj tried to conspire for a revolt, and was then awarded the death penalty. This battle was the most important battle in Indian History. *In 1194 AD, Muhammad Ghori defeated Kannauj’s Gahadavala King Jayachandra in the battle of Chandawar . Chandawar is situated in present Firozabad district (U.P.) near banks of Yamuna. *Coins issued by Ghori had image of Goddess Laxmi and Kalma was inscribed in Arabic on some other. *Soon after the victories of Muhammad Ghori ‘Iqta system’ was introduced in Northern India. *Muhammad Ghori appointed Qutb Al-Din Aybak, (also spelled Qutbuddin Aibak, Qutb-Ud-Din-Aybak) in 1192 AD as incharge of his Indian territories. He played a signiﬁ cant role in the second battle of Tarain of 1192 AD. Pleased with his works, Ghori appointed him the administrator of Kuhram and Samana. He controlled the administration of Northern parts of India as Ghori’s representative till 1206 AD. In this period, Aybak expanded the Turkish power in Northern India. *Ghori or Aybak never thought of conquering Bihar and Bengal. The task was accomplished by an ordinary slave of Muhammad Ghori named Ikhtiyar-ud-din Muhammad-Bin Bakhtiyar Khalji (1193 A.D. to 1206 A.D.). He occupied the capital Odantapuri by conquering Bihar and destroyed Nalanda and Vikramshila. He invaded Bengal from 1198 A.D. to 1204-05 A.D. At that time the ruler there was Lakshmana Sena. He left the place without actually ﬁ ghting the battle. Turkish army plundered the people entering the capital city of Nadia. In the absence of the king, the city surrendered. Escaping from there Lakshmana Sena took refuge in East Bengal and ruled there for some time. *Bakhtiyar Khalji did not try to conquer complete Bengal. title: Governor/Governor General/Viceroy
intro: In the Third Battle of Panipat (1761 A.D.), Ahmad Shah Abdali defeated the Marathas. Tipu Sultan was killed in the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War in 1799 A.D. During the war of Plassey (1757 A.D.), Mir Jafar conspired against Nawab Siraj-ud-Daulah supporting Britishers. Governor/Governor General/ Viceroy *Both Civilian and Military reforms took place during the period of Robert Clive. Under the civilian reform, a ban was imposed on the gift to of ﬁ cials and controlled private trade (Clive imposed conditioned ban on accepting gifts; i.e. for accepting gifts above Rs. 1000 of value, a pre-permission of governor is necessary). Under the Military reforms, he ended ‘double batta’ for European ofﬁ cers and from January 1, 1766 AD this allowance was only granted to soldiers who served outside the boundaries of Bengal and Bihar (except Allahabad). *Under administrative reforms, Warren Hastings in 1772 A.D. ended the dual government system of Bengal by order of the Court of Directors. He transferred the State’s treasury from Murshidabad to Calcutta. Warren Hastings believed that the whole land belonged to the ruler. To reform in Revenue ﬁ eld, he chose trial and error method . Warren Hastings in 1774 A.D. was made Governor-General of Bengal by the Regulating Act 1773. The act provides for Governor-General and four consellors (“Council of four”), total ﬁ ve (including Governor-general). The Governor General was head of the government and had casting vote if equally divided. It was established to look after the affairs of Bengal. The Chairman of the Executive Council was called Governor-General. Several types of reforms in Police, Judiciary, Taxation, Faujdari related Acts etc. took place during the time of Cornwallis. *Asiatic Society of Bengal was established on 15 th January, 1784 A.D. in the tenure of Governor General Warren Hastings. *Warren Hastings and Wellesley were related to the Ring-Fence theory. *Impeachment proceedings were initiated on Hastings for injustices and atrocities committed by him but in the light of his service, proceedings which took place between the years 1788 A.D. and 1795 A.D. (until he was acquitted in April 1795) The following were the policies of Britishers towards Indian States (Princely States):- 1- Company’s struggle for equality with Indian provinces (1740-1765 AD) 2- Policy of Ring Fence (1765-1813 AD) 3- Policy of Subordinate Isolation (1813-1857 AD) 4- Policy of Subordinate Union (1858-1935 AD) 5- Policy of Equal Federation (1935-1947 AD) *Britishers developed a new system for justice delivery through hierarchical institutions consisting of Diwani and Faujdari Courts. This system was started by Warren Hastings but Cornwallis made it more rigid. He concentrated all powers in the hands of Collector. In 1787 A.D. the District Collector was made the Diwani Judge of Diwani Courts and was granted some Faujdari Powers to deliver Justice in some Faujdari cases too.* In 1790-92 AD, District Faujdari Courts with Indian Judges were abolished and in their place four Circuit Courts, three for Bengal and one for Bihar, were appointed. These Courts were headed by European of ﬁ cials and the Justice was delivered with the help of Indian Kazis and Muftis. Cornwallis initiated his rule of speciﬁ cation of law, it was a set of regulations that codiﬁ ed administrative, revenue and judicial reforms of East India Company in Bengal. *‘Cornwallis Code’ is the collection of judicial reforms by Cornwallis in 1793 A.D. This reform was based on the law of ‘Separation of Powers’. He separated Revenue and Judicial administration. The judicial and faujdari power of collector was taken back and he was entrusted with powers related to taxation only. *A new hierarchy of ofﬁ cers was created for jobs in the District Diwani Courts. District Judges were given works of Faujdari and Police too. The modern Indian Civil Services was reorganised and professionalised by Cornwallis (1793). He forbade private trade and gifts, raised salaries, separated functions and gave legal form to civil service rules; he was regarded as the reformer of civil service. Lord Cornwallis was the Governor General of Bengal from 1786 to 1793 and from 30 th July, 1805 A.D. to 5 th October, 1805 A.D. He died at Ghazipur (Uttar Pradesh) on 5 th October 1805 A.D. His grave is present in Ghazipur. *Treaty of Bassein (December, 1802) was made between Peshwa Bajirao II and Britishers. Subsidiary Alliance of Lord Wellesley was accepted by the Peshwa Bajirao II becoming the ﬁ rst Maratha chief to do so. According to subsidiary alliance, Peshwa accepted the offer of protection of English. As per the treaty, Britishers provided 6 thousands soldiers to reinstate Peshwa at Poona and the Peshwa promised lands are having revenues worth 26 lakhs annually as a payback. * Lord Wellesley (1798-1805 A.D.) cleverly used subsidiary alliance as a tool to make Indian provinces as puppets of Britishers. He did not discover this method. This method was in practice earlier also but it gradually evolved and the ﬁ nal shape was provided by Wellesley. Dupleix was the ﬁ rst European to give his Army to an Indian ruler on the promise of a ﬁ xed payment to the Company. Britishers used these tactics too. First such instances can be traced as 1765 treaty in Oudh/ Awadh (can be marked as the precursor of subsidiary alliance) where Company promised to protect the boundaries of Oudh on a ﬁ xed payment to the Company. *The evolved version of the Subsidiary Alliance of Lord Wellesley was accepted by the Princely States in the following Sequence- Hyderabad (1798 A.D. and 1800 A.D.) , Mysore (1799 A.D.), Tanjore (October 1799 A.D.), Awadh (November 1801 A.D.), Peshwa (December 1802 A.D.), Bhonsle of Nagpur/ Berar (December Indian History General Studies B–369 1803 A.D.). Sindhiya Bharatpur (1803-05) (February 1804 A.D.), Some other alliances include Jodhpur (1818), Udaipur/ Mewar (1818), Bundi (Feb., 1818), Bikaner (March, 1818) and Jaipur (April, 1818). *Lord William Bentinck in July 1828 A.D. assumed the of ﬁ ce of Governor-General of Bengal. He took some bold steps to eliminate evil social practices such as Sati system, Female Infanticide etc. On the will of Court of Directors, he tried to adopt neutral policies towards the Princely Indian States wherever possible. Mismanagement in Jaipur one time grew so high that the British Resident was attacked there but William Bentinck did not interfere. Similarly, he did not interfere in the internal matters of Jodhpur, Bundi, Kota and Bhopal when he had enough reasons to do so. Deviating from this policy, he placed Mysore (in 1831 A.D.) and provinces of Kurg (1834 A.D.) and Kachhar (in 1832 A.D.) under British Empire because of extreme mismanagement prevailing there. *During the seven- year rule of William Bentinck (1828-35 A.D.) the old policies of war and annexation were abandoned or reduced. William Bentinck is remembered for his contributions in the ﬁ eld of Administrative and Social Reforms. *By the Charter Act of 1833 an attempt was made towards totally centralised Administration. Governor-General of Bengal became Governor-General of India through this Act. Captain Sleeman was appointed by the William Bentinck to tackle the Thug Activities. He arrested 1562 thugs between 1826 to 1835 A.D. Many of them hanged and the rest of them were exiled. By 1839 A.D., the organiZed nature of Thugi ended. *By the declaration of 1789 A.D. the export of slaves from Bengal was stopped. Acts related to slaves were formulated in 1811 A.D. and 1823 A.D. The Charter Act of 1833 A.D. emphasized on formulating law by the Governor to end slavery as soon as possible. By 1843 A.D. slavery was declared illegal in most part of British India (it removed the enforceability of slave property in civil courts). In 1860 A.D., Indian Penal Code declared slavery as a crime. (IPC was repealed and Bhartiya Nyay Samhita came into force in 2024). *Anglo-Nepal War (1814-16 A.D.) took place during the time of Governor-General Lord Hastings (1813-23 A.D.) which ended with Sugauli’s Treaty. *In 1854 James Outram was made British resident of Oudh replacing Sleeman. He said the administration of Oudh is very polluted and the condition of the people was miserable. This report of Outram emerged as the base for the annexation of Awadh. Lord Dalhousie (1848-56 A.D.) blamed Nawab of Awadh Wajid Ali Shah for maladministration and, in February 1856 A.D., Awadh was annexed by Britishers. The States that were annexed through the policy of Doctrine of Lapse are - Satara (1848), Jaitpur and Sambalpur (1849), Baghat (1850), Udaipur (1852), Jhansi (1853), Nagpur (1854) etc. *Lord Dalhousie formulated the ﬁ rst comprehensive Railway Policy for India in 1853 and strongly promoted railway expansion, though the earliest railway proposals predated his tenure (like early plan of 1832 and Lord Hardinge 1844 plan etc.). The ﬁ rst railway line was laid between Bombay to Thane in 1853 A.D. The Great Indian Peninsula Railway started the train travel in India. *Main Reason for the development of railways was to export raw materials from the inner parts of the country to different Ports of India and also open Indian markets to British manufactured goods. Its second objective was the swift movement of Army in remote and distant areas to easily suppress any kind of revolt taking place in any part of the country. *Railway expansion in India accelerated particulary between 1880 and 1900, while Lord Curzon’s contribution was mainly administrative such as the establishment of the ‘Railway Board’ in 1905. *During Dalhousie a separate Public Work Department was established and a signiﬁ cant amount was spent on public work through this body. *With the efforts of Ishwarchandra Vidyasagar, Lord Canning in 1856 A.D., passed Hindu Widow Remarriage Act. According to Act XV (15) of 1856, widow remarriage and the Child born to that marriage was legalized. Dhondo Keshav Karve and Vishnu Shashtri were two propagators of widow remarriage. Dhondo Keshav in 1896 A.D. established a widow Ashram in Poona. On August 2, 1858 the British Parliament passed the Government of India Act 1858, transferring British power over India from East India Company. The act legally abolished the company and created the secretary of State. This act led to Queen’s Proclamation. * Queen’s Proclamation of 1858 was the most important result of the 1857 revolt. This proclamation was announced on 1 st November, 1858 AD by Lord Canning at a Court held in Allahabad. The 1858 Act ended the Company rule and put the affairs of India under the direct control of the British Crown. Lord Canning was made ﬁ rst Viceroy of India. Queen Victoria was made the ruler of India in 1858 AD. A Grand Delhi Darbar organized in January 1877 AD. This Grand Durbar was organised by Lord Lytton, following the ‘Royal Titles Act 1876. During this, Queen Victoria was proclaimed ‘Empress/Sovereign of India’ & conferred with the title Kaiser-e-Hind (Qaiser-i-Hind). *Under Governor-General Auckland, ﬁ rst Anglo-Afghan war took place in 1839-1842 A.D. Lord Lytton was the Governor-General when second Anglo-Afghan war broke in 1878-1880 A.D. By Act-V of 1843 Slavery was abolished (removed legal enforce ability) by Governor-General of India Lord Ellenborough. During his tenure (1842-44 AD) in March 1843 AD Sindh was fully merged into British Empire. The policy of Masterly Inactivity in Anglo-Afghan relations was started during Lord Ellenborough and continued till Lord North Brooke. This period is called the Period of Masterly Inactivity. This policy is often recognized with John Lawrence because during his time at the ofﬁ ce, he got full chance to follow this policy and evolution of this policy took place in his time only. Masterly Inactivity word is taken from an Article published by J.W.S. Wiley. *First Census took place in 1872 A.D. during Lord Mayo (1869-72 A.D.). Proper census took place in 1881 A.D. during Lord Rippon. Lord Mayo (1869-72 A.D.) was killed during an excursion in Andaman and Nicobar Islands group by a prisoner named Sher Ali Afridi. Mayo was the Viceroy who was killed while holding the ofﬁ ce. In 1876 A.D., Lytton became Viceroy and changed his policies towards Afghanistan. *Vernacular Press Act of 1878 A.D. was passed during Lord Lytton. This Act is also called the Gagging Act. (some historians also called this as silencing act due to its strict censorship). Sir Erskine Perry termed this act as a dangerous step towards India’s right to expression. Sri S.N. Banerjee termed this act as lightning from the sky. * Sir C.P. Ilbert who was the law member of Viceroy executive council, on 2 nd February, 1883 in Legislative council presented a bill known as Ilbert Bill. This Bill was aimed at equalizing both European and Indian Judges so that Indian judges can hereby try a cases involving British subjects in various criminal cases changing the decade-old provision of barring Indian civil servants from doing so. This Bill was aimed at ending any judicial disqualiﬁ cation based on races. The Bill faced a severe opposition by Britishers as they perceived this as an attack on their privileges. *Lord Ripon is believed to be most pro- Indian Viceroy of British India. He made some lenient laws in favour of children employed in factories numbering 100 or more, this was called as First Factory Act, 1881. According to this act, a ban was imposed on the employment of children below 7 years in factories and the working hours of children aged 7 to 12 years were reduced to 9 hours daily and they got 4 holidays in a month. Second Factory Act, 1891 made week holidays possible. Lord Ripon is known as the father of the local government. Charles Metcalfe removed the restrictions on the press, he is also known as the liberator of Indian Press. In 1784 A.D., Sir William Jones founded Asiatic Society in Calcutta and steps were taken towards Archaeological Survey of India. Alexander Cunningham was appointed as the Archaeological Surveyor in 1861. In 1871, Archaeological Survey was made a separate body and Cunningham was made its Director- General. *During the tenure of Lord Curzon (1899-1905 A.D.) in 1901 The Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) became centralized and the post of DG was restored and in 1902, John Marshall (who was appointed in 1901) assumed ofﬁ ce of the Director General (DG) of this body. The Ancient Monument Preservation Act, 1904 allocated about 50,000 Pound for the protection and maintenance of the historical monuments of India. *Gopal Krishna Gokhale compared the rule of Curzon with Mughal Emperor Aurangzeb. *In November, 1905 Lord Minto replaced Lord Curzon and John Morley was made Secretary of State for India. They both proposed Morley-Minto Reforms (1909 A.D.) which granted separate electorate to Muslims. During the tenure of Lord Hardinge-II (Charles Hardinge) Capital of India was shifted to Delhi from Calcutta. He invited Queen Mary and George V in a Grand Darbar organized at Delhi which is known as third Delhi Darbar (1911 A.D.). In this Darbar, the partition of Bengal was abolished and the announcement was made for the transfer of Capital from Calcutta to Delhi.
